Indian Ocean yellowfin tuna: Cross model comparison with simulated truth and Stock Synthesis estimation model

Setup
library(opal)
library(ggplot2)

data(io_yft_data)
data(io_yft_parameters)
data(io_yft_map)
data(io_yft_reference)

ref   <- io_yft_reference
d     <- io_yft_data
n_ts  <- d$n_year
truth <- ref$truth$trajectory
ss3   <- ref$ss3$trajectory
sf    <- ref$ss3$sizefreq

# Model outputs precomputed by data-raw/generate-io-yft-vignette-cache.R, so
# the article renders without rebuilding the RTMB model
cache <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "io_yft_vignette_cache.rds", package = "opal"))
opal_m <- cache$models$age_sf

fmt <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits, big.mark = ",")
options(knitr.kable.NA = "—")
fleet_name <- function(f) sprintf("%d: %s", as.integer(f), ref$fleet_names[as.integer(f)])
last <- function(df, v) df[[v]][df$ts == max(df$ts)]

series_col <- c("Simulated truth" = "#D4AC0D", "SS3" = "grey20", "opal AGE-SF" = "#C2185B")
scale_series <- list(scale_colour_manual(values = series_col, name = NULL, drop = TRUE))
theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
            theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = element_blank()))

This article compares three views of one simulated Indian Ocean yellowfin tuna stock: the simulated truth from the spatial operating model that generated the data, the Stock Synthesis 3 (SS3) assessment of those data developed by the IATTC analyst team, and opal AGE-SF, an opal model of the same data configured to match that SS3 model as closely as opal can while every estimated parameter stays identified. How far opal AGE-SF is from SS3 measures how well opal reproduces an established assessment; how far either is from the truth measures how well a single-region assessment recovers a spatially structured stock. The differences between opal and SS3 that remain after matching their settings are described in Table 1 and Table 2.

Both the simulated data and the SS3 model come from the Spatial Stock Assessment Simulation Experiment, an international, blinded experiment in which analyst teams assessed data simulated from spatially explicit operating models without knowing the truth (Goethel et al. 2024). The IATTC team’s SS3 model was one of the assessments submitted to it.

Show code
n_catch <- sum(d$catch_obs_ysf > 0)
n_cpue  <- nrow(d$cpue_data)
n_lf    <- length(d$lf_year)
n_sf    <- length(unique(sf$data$ts))
n_comp_cells <- n_lf * d$n_len + n_sf * length(sf$bins)

The data are not a toy example. The model runs 256 quarterly time steps (1952–2015) for 16 extraction fisheries. It is conditioned on 3,642 non-zero fishery-quarter catches and fits 176 longline CPUE observations in four quarterly series, 1,114 length compositions over 39 bins of 5 cm and 127 index size compositions over 14 bins: about 45,224 composition cells in all. opal AGE-SF estimates 319 parameters, most of them the 256 quarterly recruitment deviations. This is comparable to the operational IOTC yellowfin assessment the operating model was conditioned on (Fu et al. 2018), which is also a quarterly, multi-fleet, age-structured Stock Synthesis model fitted to catch, CPUE and length compositions over a similar period.

Everything needed is bundled with the package: the data, SS3’s and the operating model’s results, and the stored opal fit.

The three models

The simulated truth

The data are replicate 4 of the Indian Ocean yellowfin operating model (OM) of the Spatial Stock Assessment Simulation Experiment. The OM was built in the Spatial Population Model software (SPM; Dunn, Rasmussen and Mormede 2015) and conditioned on Indian Ocean Tuna Commission (IOTC) fishery data (Dunn, Hoyle and Datta 2020). The experiment and its results across all participating assessments are described by Goethel et al. (2024). The OM is spatially explicit:

  • Space and time. The population lives on a 5° × 5° grid of 159 ocean cells, in quarterly time steps from 1952 to 2015 (256 quarters), with ages 1–28 quarters (28 is a plus group).
  • Recruitment. One stock with one Beverton–Holt stock–recruitment relationship (steepness 0.8) on the total spawning biomass. Quarterly recruitment strength varies (lognormal, SD 0.6), and each quarter’s recruits are spread across cells by a spatial apportionment layer with its own random variation.
  • Movement. Fish move between cells every quarter according to habitat preferences for sea surface temperature, chlorophyll-a and distance, separately for immature and mature fish. Maturation moves fish from the immature to the mature state.
  • Fishing. Seven gear-type fisheries remove their observed catches exactly, cell by cell, using exploitation rates.
  • Data. Catch (without error), longline CPUE, length frequencies and tag recaptures are simulated cell by cell.

For the experiment, the simulated data were aggregated to the four regions of the IOTC yellowfin assessment and to a single area. Because the data are simulated, the true spawning biomass and unfished spawning biomass (B0) are known. The truth files report them by assessment region; here they are summed over the whole domain. Spawning biomass is mature biomass at the start of the quarter, before fishing, in tonnes, the same definition as SS3’s and opal’s.

The SS3 model

The SS3 model (SS3 v3.24) is the IATTC analyst team’s single-region estimation model for the experiment, built by Mark N. Maunder, Haikun Xu and Carolina Minte-Vera. It treats each quarter as a model “year”, so it runs 256 time steps. It keeps the four-region structure in its fleets: its 16 extraction fisheries are gear × region combinations (for example, fishing_ll_1 to fishing_ll_4 are longline in regions 1–4). Its mean length-at-age is the OM’s own (Fu et al. 2018, after Fonteneau and Gascuel 2008), so growth is known exactly. Selectivity is age-based, and the longline survey has both a CPUE index and generalised size compositions.

opal AGE-SF

The bundled opal inputs were produced from SS3’s data, control, parameter and report files by an SS3-to-opal converter (opal-sandbox, code/rtmb). They reconcile exactly with SS3 for catch, the index, the length compositions and biology (M, weight, maturity and spawning potential at age). opal takes the same time steps (n_year = 256, n_season = 1) and SS3’s ages 1–28, so the opal age index equals the SS3 age.

Show code
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  quantity = c("Time steps (quarters)", "Ages", "Extraction fisheries",
               "Index series (longline CPUE, one per quarter)",
               "Fisheries with length compositions", "Length bins",
               "Index size-composition bins"),
  value = c(n_ts, d$n_age, 16, 4, length(d$lf_fishery_f), d$n_len, length(sf$bins))),
  col.names = c("Quantity", "Value"))

The bundled inputs (io_yft_data, io_yft_parameters, io_yft_map) use opal’s default length-based selectivity. AGE-SF changes them in two ways, shown in Building AGE-SF: it uses SS3’s age-based selectivity curves, and it fits SS3’s index size compositions with SS3’s weight. Other differences between SS3 and opal stay, as structural choices rather than settings to match.

How the three differ

The population and fishing processes:

The estimation choices, which only the two assessments have:

Catch timing is the largest difference. At SS3’s own parameter values, it alone moves opal’s spawning biomass by up to 10%, because under heavy catch opal ends each quarter with more fish than the Baranov equation leaves. The priors are kept on purpose (see How we got here).

Building AGE-SF

Growth

The bundled inputs already use SS3’s age-specific K growth. (The first conversion used opal’s single-k Schnute curve, which was 5–16 cm too long at ages 4–8 and moved the fitted stock size well away from SS3’s; opal now implements GrowthModel 3 through get_growth().)

Show code
p <- io_yft_parameters
laa_opal <- get_growth(d$n_age, d$A1, d$A2, exp(p$log_L1), exp(p$log_L2), p$log_k,
                       min_age = d$min_age, log_k_mult = p$log_k_mult,
                       k_mult_ages = d$k_mult_ages,
                       plus_group_adjust = isTRUE(d$growth_plus_group_adjust))

opal’s mean length-at-age differs from SS3’s by at most 0.0005 cm.

Age-based selectivity

SS3 uses double normal curves (age_selex pattern 20) for the fisheries, mirrors (pattern 15) for fisheries 15 and 16, and a logistic curve (pattern 12) for the longline index. sel_basis_f = 2 evaluates opal’s curves directly on age, and convert_ss3_selex_to_rtmb(basis = "age") converts SS3’s estimated parameters, held in io_yft_reference, to opal’s par_sel scale:

Show code
sp  <- ref$ss3$sel_par
pat <- ref$ss3$sel_pattern

# SS3 fleet whose parameters each opal fishery uses: fisheries 1-16 are SS3
# fleets 1-16 (15 and 16 mirror 14 through pattern 15), and the four
# quarterly index series 17-20 are SS3's survey, fleet 17.
ss3_fleet <- c(seq_len(16), rep(17L, 4))
mirror <- pat$pattern[ss3_fleet] == 15L
ss3_fleet[mirror] <- pat$special[ss3_fleet[mirror]]
ss3_pars <- t(vapply(ss3_fleet, function(fl) {
  v <- sp$value[sp$fleet == fl]
  c(v, rep(0, 6 - length(v)))
}, numeric(6)))

d_age <- io_yft_data
d_age$sel_basis_f <- rep(2L, d_age$n_fishery)
p_age <- io_yft_parameters
p_age$par_sel <- convert_ss3_selex_to_rtmb(ss3_pars, d_age$sel_type_f,
                                           sel_lengths = d_age$len_mid,
                                           basis = "age", sel_ages = d_age$age_a)

SS3’s final selectivity is −999 for every double normal, meaning “no adjustment”: the descending limb is the plain normal curve. convert_ss3_selex_to_rtmb() turns −999 into −9, which pulls the whole limb down. Setting the final selectivity to the unadjusted curve’s own value at the oldest age reproduces “no adjustment” exactly at the starting values (the final selectivity is fixed, so this is an approximation once the peak or descending width move):

Show code
# Unadjusted descending limb at the oldest age, as in sel_double_normal()
dn_unadjusted_end <- function(par, x) {
  n <- length(x)
  bin_width <- x[2] - x[1]
  peak <- mean(x) + par[1] * sd(x)
  peak2 <- peak + bin_width + (0.99 * x[n] - peak - bin_width) / (1 + exp(-par[2]))
  exp(-(x[n] - peak2)^2 / (exp(par[4]) * sd(x)^2))
}
for (f in which(d_age$sel_type_f == 2L & ss3_pars[, 6] <= -999)) {
  p_age$par_sel[f, 6] <- max(qlogis(dn_unadjusted_end(p_age$par_sel[f, ], d_age$age_a)), -20)
}

The map estimates every selectivity parameter SS3 estimated (phase > 0), with SS3’s mirrors. On the age scale, SS3’s plateau and ascending-width parameters for several fisheries are near −10 to −15, outside opal’s default par_sel bounds of ±7, so the bounds are widened to SS3’s ±20:

Show code
est <- matrix(NA_integer_, d_age$n_fishery, 6)
k <- 0L
for (fl in unique(ss3_fleet)) {
  cols <- sp$par[sp$fleet == fl & sp$phase > 0]
  ids <- k + seq_along(cols)
  k <- k + length(cols)
  for (f in which(ss3_fleet == fl)) est[f, cols] <- ids
}
map_age <- io_yft_map
map_age$par_sel <- factor(as.vector(est))

age_bounds <- function(parameters, map, lim = 20) {
  active <- unlist(lapply(names(parameters), function(n)
    rep(n, if (is.null(map[[n]])) length(parameters[[n]]) else nlevels(droplevels(map[[n]])))))
  b <- get_bounds(list(par = setNames(numeric(length(active)), active)), parameters)
  b$lower[b$parameter == "par_sel"] <- -lim
  b$upper[b$parameter == "par_sel"] <- lim
  b
}

At SS3’s parameters, opal’s age-based curves reproduce SS3’s selectivity-at-age:

Show code
sel0 <- get_selectivity(d_age, p_age$par_sel, pla = NULL, len_mid = d_age$len_mid,
                        age_a = d_age$age_a)[, 1, ]
s0 <- data.frame(fishery = rep(seq_len(nrow(sel0)), times = ncol(sel0)),
                 age = rep(d_age$age_a, each = nrow(sel0)), sel = as.vector(sel0))
cmp <- merge(s0, ref$ss3$sel_age, by = c("fishery", "age"), suffixes = c("_opal", "_ss3"))

The largest difference over all fisheries and ages is 0.0010; 58 selectivity parameters are estimated.

Index size compositions

SS3’s generalised size compositions for the survey use 14 bins with lower edges 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90, 100, 110, 120, 130, 140, 150, 160 cm, in numbers, with 127 observations and sample sizes of 5–35. SS3 puts the population below 30 cm into the first bin, and the last bin is open-ended; opal’s default "accumulate" tails do both. prep_lf_data() takes the 5 cm length compositions and the size compositions as two wide tables, each on its own bins; only opal’s predictions are rebinned. In opal the index is four quarterly series, so each observation goes to the index fishery of its quarter; the four share one selectivity curve, as SS3’s survey does. SS3’s lambda of 0.51 on the size compositions becomes an lf lambda on those four fisheries.

Show code
# The bundled 5 cm compositions as a wide table of counts. lf_n carries
# SS3's variance adjustment (n / lf_var_adjust), so it is undone here for
# prep_lf_data() to reapply.
lf_wide <- function(d) {
  n_raw <- d$lf_n * d$lf_var_adjust[d$lf_fishery]
  counts <- d$lf_obs_in * n_raw
  colnames(counts) <- as.character(d$len_lower)
  data.frame(fishery = d$lf_fishery, year = d$lf_year, month = 1L, ts = d$lf_year,
             counts, check.names = FALSE)
}
# SS3's size compositions as a wide table of counts (proportion x sample size)
sizefreq_wide <- function(ref) {
  sf <- ref$ss3$sizefreq$data
  wide <- stats::reshape(sf[, c("ts", "fishery", "nsamp", "bin", "obs")],
                         idvar = c("ts", "fishery", "nsamp"), timevar = "bin",
                         direction = "wide")
  counts <- as.matrix(wide[, paste0("obs.", ref$ss3$sizefreq$bins)]) * wide$nsamp
  colnames(counts) <- as.character(ref$ss3$sizefreq$bins)
  data.frame(fishery = wide$fishery, year = wide$ts, month = 1L, ts = wide$ts,
             counts, check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
}

# Both bin schemes end at the top of the model's length grid
top <- d_age$len_bin_start + d_age$n_len * d_age$len_bin_width
d_sf <- prep_lf_data(
  d_age,
  list(lf_wide(d_age), sizefreq_wide(ref)),
  lf_switch     = d_age$lf_switch,
  lf_minbin     = d_age$lf_minbin,
  lf_maxbin     = d_age$lf_maxbin,
  lf_var_adjust = d_age$lf_var_adjust,
  lf_addtocomp  = d_age$lf_addtocomp,
  lf_upper_edge = c(top, top))

index_f <- sort(unique(d_age$cpue_data$fishery))
lf_lambda <- rep(1, d_sf$n_fishery)
lf_lambda[index_f] <- sf$lambda
d_sf$lambdas <- list(lf = lf_lambda)

At SS3’s solution (before fitting), opal’s predicted size compositions are close to SS3’s expected values:

Show code
ss3_like <- function(o, e, n) { i <- o > 0; -sum(n[i] * o[i] * log(e[i] / o[i])) }
sf_pred <- function(nm) merge(sf$data, cache$models[[nm]]$sizefreq,
                              by = c("fishery", "ts", "bin"))
chk <- sf_pred("age_sf_start")
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  quantity = c("Largest difference in a proportion", "Mean absolute difference",
               "SS3-style multinomial likelihood, SS3's expected values",
               "The same, opal's predictions", "SS3's reported likelihood (Report.sso)"),
  value = c(fmt(max(abs(chk$predicted - chk$expected)), 4),
            fmt(mean(abs(chk$predicted - chk$expected)), 4),
            fmt(ss3_like(chk$obs, chk$expected, chk$nsamp), 1),
            fmt(ss3_like(chk$obs, chk$predicted, chk$nsamp), 1), "1,067.4")),
  col.names = c("At SS3's solution", "Value"))
At SS3’s solution Value
Largest difference in a proportion 0.0102
Mean absolute difference 0.0014
SS3-style multinomial likelihood, SS3’s expected values 1,067.5
The same, opal’s predictions 1,064.0
SS3’s reported likelihood (Report.sso) 1,067.4

The remaining difference is the timing: SS3 takes the survey at mid-quarter, opal at the start. (The SS3-style likelihood is −Σ N o log(e / o); opal’s multinomial differs by a constant.)

Fit

AGE-SF is fitted in two steps: first without the size compositions (AGE), from SS3’s solution, then with them, from AGE’s estimates. Fitting takes several minutes, so the article uses the stored fit, made from exactly these inputs. data-raw/generate-io-yft-fits.R also polishes the optimum with Newton steps and runs opal_check() with a gradient tolerance of 1e-4.

Show code
control <- list(eval.max = 10000, iter.max = 10000)
age <- opal_fit(opal_obj(d_age, p_age, map_age, bounds = age_bounds(p_age, map_age),
                         control = control), n_passes = 2L)
p_start <- opal_rtmb(age)$env$parList(age$fit$opt$par)
age_sf <- opal_fit(opal_obj(d_sf, p_start, map_age, bounds = age_bounds(p_start, map_age),
                            control = control), n_passes = 2L)

# The stored fit
age_sf <- opal_read(system.file("extdata", "io_yft_age_sf_fit.rds", package = "opal"))
summary(age_sf)
Show code
v <- opal_m$fit
w <- opal_m$nll_w
knitr::kable(data.frame(

            fmt(w[["sizefreq"]], 1), fmt(w[["recruitment"]], 1), fmt(w[["prior"]], 1),
            formatC(v$max_gradient, format = "e", digits = 1),

How we got here

AGE-SF is the last of a sequence of opal fits, each making one change from the one before. SS3-SEL holds selectivity at SS3’s estimates; LEN is the bundled inputs (io_yft_map), with opal’s length-based selectivity estimated; AGE-SF-NP is SS3’s configuration exactly, with the priors switched off as well.

Show code
br <- cache$bridge
h <- ref$history[2, ]
bridge <- rbind(
  data.frame(model = "SS3-SEL", change = "SS3's selectivity held fixed",
             sel_free = 0L, B0 = h$B0, dep = h$terminal_depletion, check = NA),
  data.frame(model = br$model, change = br$change, sel_free = br$sel_free, B0 = br$B0,
             dep = br$terminal_depletion,
             check = ifelse(br$passes, "passed",
                            ifelse(br$positive_hessian, "failed", "failed (Hessian)"))),
  data.frame(model = "SS3", change = NA, sel_free = NA, B0 = ref$ss3$ssb0,
             dep = last(ss3, "static_dep"), check = NA),
  data.frame(model = "Simulated truth", change = NA, sel_free = NA, B0 = ref$truth$b0,
             dep = last(truth, "static_dep"), check = NA))
bridge$B0 <- bridge$B0 / ref$ss3$ssb0
bridge$model[bridge$model == "AGE-SF"] <- "**AGE-SF**"
knitr::kable(bridge, digits = c(0, 0, 0, 2, 3, 0), row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Fit", "Change from the row above", "Selectivity parameters",
                           "B0 / SS3 B0", "Terminal SSB / B0", "opal_check()"))
Fit Change from the row above Selectivity parameters B0 / SS3 B0 Terminal SSB / B0 opal_check()
SS3-SEL SS3’s selectivity held fixed 0 1.03 0.404 —
LEN Estimate opal’s length-based selectivity 49 0.88 0.307 passed
AGE SS3’s age-based curves and mirrors; every parameter SS3 estimated 58 0.84 0.298 passed
AGE-SF Add SS3’s index size compositions (lambda 0.51) 58 0.88 0.364 passed
AGE-SF-NP Switch off the priors (SS3’s lambda of 0) 38 0.91 0.374 failed (Hessian)
SS3 — — 1.00 0.399 —
Simulated truth — — 0.84 0.468 —
Show code
b <- setNames(seq_len(nrow(br)), br$model)
  • Held at SS3’s selectivity, opal reproduces SS3’s stock size closely. Estimating selectivity lowers it, whether the curves are opal’s length-based ones (LEN) or SS3’s own age-based ones (AGE), so the selectivity basis is not what separates opal from SS3.
  • The index size compositions inform the index’s selectivity, which otherwise only the CPUE trend informs. They move opal’s depletion from 0.298 to 0.364, towards SS3’s.
  • Switching off the priors, as SS3 does, leaves 20 selectivity parameters with a flat likelihood (plateau widths at a single age, knife-edge limbs, and the plateau and descending limb of asymptotic fisheries). AGE-SF-NP holds them fixed, and its Hessian is still not positive definite, so its standard errors cannot be used; SS3, run without a Hessian, does not report on this. Its stock status differs little from AGE-SF’s. Without priors the likelihood also has more than one optimum: started from SS3’s solution rather than AGE’s estimates, AGE-SF-NP stops at a worse optimum with a larger stock. AGE-SF keeps opal’s priors, which identify every parameter SS3 estimated.

Stock status

Fits to the data

The truth has no fits to the data, and its selectivity is defined by gear and cell, so this section compares SS3 and opal only.

Index

Show code
cp <- d$cpue_data
idx <- data.frame(ts = cp$ts, fishery = cp$fishery, obs = cp$value, se = cp$se,
                  pred = opal_m$cpue$pred)
pred <- rbind(data.frame(ts = ref$ss3$cpue$ts, fishery = ref$ss3$cpue$fishery,
                         value = ref$ss3$cpue$expected, series = "SS3"),
              data.frame(ts = idx$ts, fishery = idx$fishery, value = idx$pred,
                         series = "opal AGE-SF"))
pred$series <- factor(pred$series, names(series_col))
ggplot() +
  geom_linerange(data = idx, aes(ts, ymin = obs * exp(-1.96 * se), ymax = obs * exp(1.96 * se)),
                 colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(data = idx, aes(ts, obs), size = 1, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(data = pred, aes(ts, value, colour = series), linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ fishery, ncol = 1, labeller = as_labeller(fleet_name)) +
  scale_series +
  labs(x = "Time step (quarter)", y = "Index (mean = 1 per series)")
Show code
rmse <- function(o, p) sqrt(mean((log(o) - log(p))^2))
knitr::kable(data.frame(model = c("SS3", "opal AGE-SF"),
                        rmse = c(rmse(ref$ss3$cpue$obs, ref$ss3$cpue$expected),
                                 rmse(idx$obs, idx$pred))),
             digits = 4, col.names = c("Model", "RMSE of log index residuals"))
Model RMSE of log index residuals
SS3 0.0646
opal AGE-SF 0.0642

Length compositions

Show code
agg <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(d$lf_fishery_f), function(j) {
  obs <- d$lf_obs_data$obs[[j]]
  obs <- obs / rowSums(obs)
  n   <- d$lf_n_fi[[j]]
  data.frame(fishery = d$lf_fishery_f[j], bin = d$len_lower,
             observed = colSums(obs * n) / sum(n))
}))
lines <- rbind(
  data.frame(fishery = ref$ss3$lf$fishery, bin = ref$ss3$lf$bin,
             value = ref$ss3$lf$expected, series = "SS3"),
  data.frame(fishery = opal_m$lf$fishery, bin = opal_m$lf$bin,
             value = opal_m$lf$predicted, series = "opal AGE-SF"))
lines$series <- factor(lines$series, names(series_col))
width <- diff(d$len_lower[1:2])
ggplot() +
  geom_col(data = agg, aes(bin + width / 2, observed), fill = "grey80", width = width) +
  geom_line(data = lines, aes(bin + width / 2, value, colour = series), linewidth = 0.6) +

Index size compositions

  data.frame(bin = as.numeric(names(a)), value = as.numeric(a / sum(a)))
}
p_sf <- sf_pred("age_sf")
lines_sf <- rbind(data.frame(agg_sf(p_sf, "expected"), series = "SS3"),

ggplot() +

Selectivity

Show code
sa <- rbind(data.frame(ref$ss3$sel_age, series = "SS3"),
            data.frame(opal_m$sel_age, series = "opal AGE-SF"))
sa$series <- factor(sa$series, names(series_col))
ggplot(sa[sa$fishery <= 17, ], aes(age, sel, colour = series)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ fishery, ncol = 4, labeller = as_labeller(fleet_name)) +
  scale_series +
  labs(x = "Age (quarters)", y = "Selectivity")
Show code
a50 <- function(sa) {
  s <- sa[sa$fishery == 17, ]
  stats::approx(s$sel, s$age, 0.5, ties = "ordered")$y
}
a50_ss3 <- a50(ref$ss3$sel_age)
a50_opal <- a50(opal_m$sel_age)

Fisheries 15 and 16 mirror 14, and panel 17 stands for all four quarterly index series. The index reaches 50% selectivity at 8.3 quarters in opal and 8.1 in SS3; SS3’s estimate sits at its lower bound of 8 quarters, which opal does not impose.

Summary

Show code
dep_t <- last(truth, "static_dep")
dep_s <- last(ss3, "static_dep")
dep_o <- last(opal_tr, "static_dep")
  • Against the truth. Neither single-region assessment is the truth. The operating model has movement among 159 cells and spatially varying recruitment, which neither represents. SS3’s B0 is 1.19 × the true B0 and opal AGE-SF’s 1.04 ×; terminal depletion is 0.399 (SS3) and 0.364 (opal), against a true 0.468.
  • Against SS3. With SS3’s growth, selectivity curves and mirrors, index size compositions and lambda, opal AGE-SF’s B0 is 0.88 × SS3’s, and its spawning biomass differs from SS3’s by 14.6% on average. The fit converges and passes opal_check().
  • What remains. The rest of the gap to SS3 lies in the structural differences that stay: catch removed at the start of the quarter rather than through it (up to 10% of spawning biomass at SS3’s own parameters), four quarterly catchabilities rather than one, and unconstrained recruitment deviations. It also depends on which optimum each model is in. Removing opal’s priors as well (AGE-SF-NP, SS3’s configuration) changes the stock status little, but leaves some selectivity parameters unidentified.

Credit and references

The simulated example and the SS3 estimation model both come from the Spatial Stock Assessment Simulation Experiment. The SS3 model was developed by the IATTC analyst team (Mark N. Maunder, Haikun Xu and Carolina Minte-Vera, Inter-American Tropical Tuna Commission) as their submission to it. The experiment’s design, its operating models and the evaluation of the submitted assessments, including theirs, are described in:

  • Goethel, D.R., et al. (2024). ‘Drivin’ with your eyes closed’: Results from an international, blinded simulation experiment to evaluate spatial stock assessments. Fish and Fisheries 25(3): 471–490. https://doi.org/10.1111/faf.12819

The age-specific K growth model is Stock Synthesis’ GrowthModel 3:

  • Methot, R.D. Jr., and Wetzel, C.R. (2013). Stock synthesis: A biological and statistical framework for fish stock assessment and fishery management. Fisheries Research 142: 86–99. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fishres.2012.10.012

The data and the simulated truth are from replicate 4 of the Indian Ocean yellowfin operating model (https://github.com/aaronmberger-nwfsc/Spatial-Assessment-Modeling-Workshop). The IOTC working-party papers below have no DOI, so they link to the IOTC document archive where a copy is available:

  • Dunn, A., Rasmussen, S. and Mormede, S. (2015). Spatial Population Model. NIWA Technical Report 138.
  • Dunn, A., Hoyle, S. and Datta, S. (2020). Development of spatially explicit operating models for yellowfin tuna populations in the Indian Ocean. IOTC-2020-WPTT22(AS)-19_Rev1. https://iotc.org/sites/default/files/documents/2020/10/IOTC-2020-WPTT22AS-19_Rev1.pdf
  • Fu, D., Langley, A., Merino, G. and Urtizberea, A. (2018). Preliminary Indian Ocean yellowfin tuna stock assessment 1950–2017 (Stock Synthesis). IOTC-2018-WPTT20-33. https://iotc.org/sites/default/files/documents/2018/10/IOTC-2018-WPTT20-33.pdf
  • Fonteneau, A. and Gascuel, D. (2008). Growth rates and apparent growth curves, for yellowfin, skipjack and bigeye tagged and recovered in the Indian Ocean during the IOTTP. IOTC-2008-WPTDA-08.

The SS3-to-opal converter is in https://github.com/N-DucharmeBarth/opal-sandbox (code/rtmb); the bundled data were exported by code/rtmb/scripts/04-export-io-yft-for-opal.r at commit 047af02, and SS3’s size compositions and lambdas by code/rtmb/scripts/06-export-io-yft-sizefreq-for-opal.r. The opal outputs shown were computed with opal 0.1.1 (commit fdcd449) by data-raw/generate-io-yft-fits.R and data-raw/generate-io-yft-vignette-cache.R.
